title: Deacon Readiness
subtitle: An honest look at your life against the marks the New Testament sets for the ministry of service.
intro:
This is not a form you fill out to earn a title. It is a quiet self-examination before God, with Acts chapter six and First Timothy chapter three open beside you. The deacon was never meant to be a lesser officer or a stepping stone to something greater. It is the office of proven, faithful, hands-on service, and the early church chose people for it precisely because their character was already tested and trusted.

Answer honestly, as you actually are. No one sees this but you and God. The aim is not to qualify yourself but to see clearly, so that you can pray and let the people who have watched you serve speak the truth into what you find.

questions.text: My character has been tested over time, and people who have known me for years would vouch for me without hesitation.
I am dignified and trustworthy, and I do not say one thing to one person and something different to another.
I am not greedy, and I would never let the handling of money or resources be touched by self-interest.
I hold the deep truths of the faith with a clear conscience, and my belief and my conduct are not at war with each other.
I am not a heavy drinker or governed by any appetite that would compromise my judgment.
I have a track record of actually serving people, not just talking about service from a distance.
I can be trusted with something hard or unglamorous and finish it without being chased or thanked.
I keep confidences, and I do not carry gossip or use what I learn in service as currency.
My household is in order, and those nearest me would describe my home as marked by care rather than chaos.
I notice the overlooked people, the ones who fall through the gaps, the way the early deacons noticed the neglected widows.
I can serve under the direction of others without needing recognition or resenting the ones who lead.
I am full of the Spirit and of practical wisdom, and people instinctively trust me with delicate situations.
I would take this office to wash feet, not to gain standing or a path toward something more visible.
I am willing to be examined first and entrusted second, the way the New Testament requires.

bands.label: Not yet, and that is not a failure
bands.body:
The honest reading is that the proven character the office requires is not yet in place, and that is a kind word, not a closed door. Acts six is careful about this. The early church did not pick the eager or the available. They picked people already known to be full of the Spirit and wisdom, people whose service had already left a mark.

Do not hear this as rejection. Hear it as direction. The ministry of service is learned by serving, quietly, before anyone names you a deacon. Find the unglamorous work no one is fighting over and do it faithfully for a long time.

That is not the consolation prize. That is the whole training. The deacons of Acts six became trusted by being trustworthy in plain sight, year after year, until the church simply recognized what was already true.

bands.label: Service is beginning, but it is not yet proven
bands.body:
There is genuine evidence that God is shaping you toward this kind of service, and there are also gaps that are not ready to carry the trust the office assumes. That mixture is honest, and most people who love the church live somewhere in it. The danger is mistaking a willing heart for a tested one.

Look closely at your lowest answers. Maybe it is consistency, maybe it is how you handle money or confidences, maybe it is a home that is more strained than settled. First Timothy says deacons must first be tested. The testing happens in exactly these places, and it happens before the title, not after.

Bring these to someone who has watched you serve. Let them tell you the truth. Service that is only half-proven is not ready to be trusted with the vulnerable people a deacon is meant to protect.

bands.label: The marks are largely here, keep listening
bands.body:
Much of what the New Testament asks of a deacon appears to be present and tested in you. That should make you sober, not satisfied. The closer you come to being trusted with the care of people, the more honestly you should look at the places you would rather not examine.

Do not dismiss the one or two answers that came back lower. They are the places that will be exposed when the work is hard, the resources are tight, and no one is watching. The ministry of service is full of exactly those moments.

Now is the time to invite examination instead of avoiding it. Ask the people you serve alongside to speak plainly about your character, your money, your follow-through, and your home. A servant the church can name with confidence is steady. A servant who names himself is not.

bands.label: The marks are here, let the church confirm it
bands.body:
By your own honest reckoning, the tested character and proven service the New Testament describes have taken root in you. That is a serious and quiet thing, not something to announce. It is something to carry toward the people who have watched you work.

No web page can set you apart for this. The early church laid hands on its deacons only after the whole body had recognized them. Take this result to your pastor and your leaders and the people you have served beside, and ask them to test it honestly, including the corners you suspect are softer than they appear.

If the marks are truly here, the church will see them, and you will not have to push. Submit to that. The same humility that makes a person fit to serve is the humility that lets the body, not the candidate, speak the final word.

closing: This is a mirror for discernment before God, and only the local body that has watched you serve can confirm a calling. A web tool never can.
